intro: Buying a home in Alaska involves more than finding a property at the right price. Local property taxes, heating expenses, insurance requirements and the availability of mortgage financing can all affect affordability.

Our Alaska mortgage calculator helps you estimate your monthly housing payment using your purchase price, down payment, interest rate and loan term. Include property taxes, homeowners insurance and applicable mortgage insurance to build a realistic budget before purchasing a home.

sections.heading: Quick Answer: How Much Is a Mortgage Payment in Alaska?

blocks.markdown:
A $350,000 home purchased with a 20% down payment and a 30-year mortgage at a 6% fixed interest rate would have a monthly principal and interest payment of approximately $1,678.74.

Here is an illustrative payment breakdown:
This example assumes no private mortgage insurance or HOA fees. Actual taxes, insurance premiums and interest rates depend on the property and your financing arrangements.

Alaska's housing market includes urban properties in Anchorage, homes in Fairbanks, coastal communities such as Juneau and remote settlements with limited transportation access.

According to the [US Census Bureau's Alaska QuickFacts](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/AK), the median value of owner-occupied homes was $352,900 during the 2020–2024 survey period.

Median selected monthly homeowner costs among households with mortgages reached $2,229, while the owner-occupied housing rate was 66.8%.

These historical statistics help establish a starting point for financial planning, but housing prices vary considerably between communities.

Construction materials, transportation requirements, available land and access to utilities can influence both purchase prices and ongoing maintenance expenses.

Before choosing a home price for the calculator, research properties in your intended community rather than relying exclusively on statewide housing figures.

sections.heading: How to Use the Alaska Mortgage Calculator

blocks.markdown:
Enter the expected purchase price of your property and the amount you intend to contribute as a down payment.

Next, select your repayment term and enter the annual mortgage interest rate quoted by your lender.

Add your expected annual property taxes and insurance premiums. If your property has association fees or requires mortgage insurance, include those amounts.

Review the estimated monthly payment and experiment with different loan terms or down payment amounts.

The calculator also provides information about your outstanding loan balance and interest expenses over time.

For properties in remote areas, remember that the calculator may not automatically include heating fuel, water delivery, transportation and other location-specific living costs.

sections.heading: How Property Taxes Work in Alaska

blocks.markdown:
Alaska has an unusual property taxation system because many areas do not impose a municipal property tax.

According to the [Alaska Office of the State Assessor](https://www.commerce.alaska.gov/web/dcra/officeofthestateassessor/alaskataxfacts), only 24 municipalities levied property taxes as reported in its November 2026 update.

However, buyers in municipalities that collect property taxes should expect those charges to contribute to their annual ownership expenses.

Property taxes generally depend on the locally assessed property value and applicable millage rate.

For example, suppose your property has an assessed taxable value of $350,000 and an illustrative millage rate of 12 mills.

Annual property tax would be:

$350,000 × 0.012 = $4,200

This equals $350 per month.

The actual assessment and millage rate must come from the relevant municipality.

### Property tax exemptions for Alaska homeowners

Alaska provides qualifying senior homeowners and disabled veterans with an exemption on the first $150,000 of assessed property value, subject to applicable eligibility requirements.

Municipalities may have additional provisions.

Contact the local assessor to determine whether you qualify and when an application must be submitted.

Never assume that a property advertised in a low-tax location will automatically qualify for an exemption.

Insurance is particularly important when purchasing property in Alaska because local environmental conditions may create additional risks.

Freezing temperatures, heavy snowfall, earthquake exposure and flooding can affect properties differently depending on their construction and location.

The [Alaska Division of Insurance's earthquake insurance guidance](https://www.commerce.alaska.gov/web/ins/Consumers/HomeInsurance/EarthquakeInsurance.aspx) explains that most standard residential insurance policies exclude earthquake damage.

Buyers should compare separate earthquake coverage where appropriate and carefully review deductibles, coverage limits and exclusions.

A property in a remote community may also present challenges when arranging repairs or sourcing replacement building materials.

When obtaining insurance quotes, focus on the estimated cost of rebuilding the home rather than assuming that its purchase price represents an appropriate coverage limit.

Use the annual cost of all relevant policies when estimating your housing expenses.
The following estimates assume a 20% down payment, a 6% fixed annual interest rate and a 30-year repayment term.

These figures exclude property taxes, insurance, HOA fees and other homeownership expenses.

A larger down payment reduces the amount borrowed. A lower interest rate reduces borrowing costs without requiring a change in the purchase price.

sections.heading: Alaska Housing Finance Corporation Mortgage Programs

blocks.markdown:
The Alaska Housing Finance Corporation, commonly known as Alaska Housing or AHFC, offers several financing programs through approved lenders.

### First Home and First Home Limited

The [AHFC first-time homebuyer programs](https://www.ahfc.us/buy/loan-programs/first-time-loans) provide mortgage options for eligible borrowers.

First Home Limited offers potentially favorable interest rates to applicants meeting applicable income and property acquisition limits.

First-time buyers generally must not have owned a primary residence during the preceding three years, although certain exceptions apply.

Compare both programs with ordinary conventional mortgage offers before selecting financing.

### Rural Owner-Occupied Loan

The [Alaska Housing Rural Loan program](https://www.ahfc.us/buy/loan-programs/rural-programs) supports eligible residential purchases and renovations in qualifying small communities.

Its financing structure can differ from standard conventional loans. For example, different interest rate treatment can apply to portions of a loan above the program's specified threshold.

Because these arrangements may involve blended rates, request a complete payment estimate from an approved lender rather than assuming the standard mortgage calculation represents the exact program payment.

### Down payment assistance

AHFC provides information about nonprofit organizations offering [down payment assistance across Alaska](https://www.ahfc.us/buy/resources/down-payment-assistance).

Assistance may depend on your community, income, loan type and available funding.

Check whether the support takes the form of a repayable loan, deferred financing or another arrangement before calculating your required cash at closing.

Conventional financing is one option for buyers who satisfy lender credit and income requirements.

Eligible military households can explore [VA-backed purchase loans](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/), which may offer financing without a down payment.

Buyers in qualifying communities may also consider [USDA rural development housing programs](https://www.rd.usda.gov/).

FHA-insured loans can provide another alternative, although upfront and ongoing mortgage insurance expenses must be included where applicable.

When comparing offers, pay attention to lender fees, property eligibility, annual percentage rates and cash requirements rather than focusing only on the advertised interest rate.

A mortgage calculator estimates financing and selected recurring housing expenses, but Alaska homeowners should also prepare for costs outside their mortgage.

### Heating and energy expenses

Heating expenses can vary substantially depending on the climate, insulation, heating system and local fuel availability.

Request historical utility bills from the seller and consider whether the property's heating equipment may require replacement.

### Remote property maintenance

Some communities have limited access to contractors, building supplies and repair services.

Budget for potential shipping charges and longer repair timelines when purchasing outside major population centers.

### Water and wastewater systems

Not every property connects to municipal utilities. Some homes rely on wells, septic systems, water delivery or other arrangements.

Understand the recurring costs, inspection requirements and maintenance obligations before finalizing your purchase.

These expenses can materially affect affordability even when the mortgage payment itself appears manageable.

sections.heading: How Much House Can You Afford in Alaska?

blocks.markdown:
Start by calculating your reliable monthly take-home income and subtracting existing living expenses.

Consider seasonal employment patterns, variable earnings and transportation costs. If you rely on overtime or seasonal income, test a conservative budget that does not assume those earnings remain constant.

Our [Alaska Paycheck Calculator](/calculators/alaska-paycheck-calculator/) can help you estimate take-home pay, while our [Debt to Income Ratio Calculator](/debt/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator/) can help you understand the relationship between debt obligations and income.

You should also maintain enough savings to cover emergency repairs and insurance deductibles.

Review the [CFPB's homebuying affordability guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/) when determining an appropriate purchase budget.

sections.heading: Closing Costs and Mortgage Rates in Alaska

blocks.markdown:
Closing costs may include lender fees, property appraisals, title services, recording fees and prepaid insurance.

Ask lenders whether additional inspections or appraisal requirements apply to your intended property, particularly in remote communities.

For mortgage rate information, consult the [AHFC published rate page](https://www.ahfc.us/buy/resources/current-rates) and obtain an individualized quote from an approved lender.

Rates may change between the initial estimate and the final mortgage agreement.

### How much is a mortgage payment on a $350,000 home in Alaska?

With a 20% down payment and a 30-year mortgage at 6%, monthly principal and interest would be approximately $1,678.74. Add local property taxes, insurance and applicable fees to estimate your total housing payment.

### Does every Alaska homeowner pay property taxes?

No. Many Alaska communities do not impose a municipal property tax. However, properties in municipalities that levy these taxes may have substantial annual bills. Confirm the applicable charges with your local assessor.

### Are special mortgage programs available for rural Alaska properties?

Yes. Alaska Housing offers rural mortgage programs for qualifying properties and borrowers in eligible small communities. Program requirements and interest rate structures can differ from conventional financing.

Use the Alaska mortgage calculator to compare financing options and determine how different purchase prices affect your monthly budget.

Remember to include heating, maintenance, insurance and other location-specific expenses when evaluating the true cost of owning a home in Alaska.
